Governance review

TLA and Treasury: who controls the funds?

Approved infrastructure funding, delivered safeguards and the control handovers that remain incomplete.

Checked 16 November 2026. This review follows 27 named Terra contracts and selected approved proposals. It is a bounded control map, not a complete inventory of ERIS property or an audit of every transaction.

The central concern is control of TLA and Treasury

These systems were funded to manage chain liquidity and community funds. ERIS delivered deployed infrastructure and the Board holds meaningful operating powers, but ERIS-associated addresses retain migration administration and registry ownership. TLA’s published one-month and three-month handover commitments remain incomplete.

A documented commitment remains incomplete

The TLA launch terms promised migration-admin transfer to Phoenix Stewardship after one month and configuration ownership after three. The named ERIS addresses still hold those roles across the reviewed TLA deployment. No approved extension was identified in the reviewed records.

Some control has transferred

ERIS proposal 9 transferred upgrade administration of the ampLUNA hub and CW20-ICS20 bridge to the Board on 25 October 2026. Their internal permissions remain separate. The Board has since exercised its upgrade authority through A292.

Application grants are a separate question. Creda, Votion and Estima funded applications; the grants alone do not establish community ownership of their software or an obligation to surrender administration. They are listed separately and are not the basis for the TLA/Treasury handover finding.

These keys are not beyond native Terra governance: an approved executable proposal can reassign administrators or migrate contracts. The available remedies have different effects and limits.

Control is not legal ownership

Scroll sideways to read all columns.

QuestionWhat the record establishes
Who owns the assets?The TLA development text describes acquired LP positions as Community Pool liquidity. User deposits and the tokens representing them remain subject to their protocol claims. A grant is funding for an agreed scope; balances, fees and technical permissions do not establish beneficial ownership or personal profit.
Who can replace a contract?Its migration administrator can authorize new code, subject to chain rules. This is a separate layer from ordinary spending approval.
Who can change settings?An internal owner or registry role controls the functions assigned to it by the deployed code. A field named owner is not a legal title deed.
Who can operate it?Controllers, voting operators, whitelist managers and executors have distinct permissions. Paying for development or operating a service does not by itself settle the permanent authority to govern it.

Software licences, IP assignments, grant conditions and any later approved variations need their own register. This review did not establish legal title to every ERIS product or find an approved blanket entitlement to retain all community-system powers indefinitely.

This is a gross contract balance, not an available-spending budget, valuation or total Foundation asset figure. Reserved grant amounts, virtual Alliance tokens, staked positions and assets in other contracts must be reconciled separately.

Could retained keys put Treasury funds at risk?

Yes: the upgrade layer creates a material route around ordinary in-contract approval rules. A compatible replacement implementation could change authorization, remove or weaken in-code veto checks, and instruct transfers of spendable assets held by the Treasury address. That is a consequence of administrator-controlled code replacement, not evidence that such a replacement or transfer has occurred. No live drain or destructive test was performed.

The same issue applies to assets held in other upgradeable contracts, including pooled user assets. Control over one contract does not automatically authorize withdrawals from every Foundation wallet or unrelated protocol. Staking, IBC, external contracts, liabilities and chain-level governance impose additional boundaries. The Board’s upgrade control of the hub and bridge is an important independent control, not a guarantee covering TLA or Treasury.

The two ERIS-labelled addresses expose single public keys in their chain account records; neither is recorded as an on-chain multisig. That does not reveal who holds the keys, whether off-chain co-signing exists, or whether one individual can act alone. The launch attribution establishes ERIS-associated roles, not private key custody.

Rejected TLA changes are not adopted policy

Whitelisting reform #4830 and pool relocation #4836 were rejected. Their proposed changes cannot be presented as new mandates, and rejection alone does not document repeal of the original handover commitments.

This is a control and delivery comparison, not a full grant-performance audit. Quarterly reporting, the conditional URA refund, full take-rate accounting and all later source revisions require separate reconciliation.

The hub handover is real, but internal powers still matter

The focused review of hub code 2726 found additional owner control over batching and unbonding timings, alongside existing fee, delegation and voting-operator settings. Poor settings could disrupt operation or delay withdrawals. The Board’s migration power provides a route to change these controls; the policy question is which settings the owner may change, under what limits and with whose approval.

P9’s execution date comes from retained primary transaction evidence; executed proposal status and current administrators were checked again. A292 is now executed, superseding older discussion-stage descriptions. The focused binary review is not a full security audit.

Why this is a governance problem

Approval rules can sit below a stronger key

Community voting and Board thresholds provide weaker assurance when another authority can replace the rules they rely on. That creates exposure to intentional misuse, key compromise and mistakes even if ordinary approvals are followed.

Responsibility and power can diverge

The Board is accountable for community assets but may depend on an outside operator for contract changes, source access or emergency recovery. A dispute or unavailable maintainer can interrupt service; an unclear handover makes that dependence difficult to assess.

The concern is structural. The evidence does not establish an intention to misuse funds, a completed theft, or legal ownership of all protocol assets by ERIS. ERIS’s maintenance rationale deserves consideration alongside the community’s right to explicit, reviewable limits on retained authority.

Source access is part of control

The Treasury launch advertised audited open-source code. The advertised erisprotocol/contracts-ve3 public repository returned 404 when checked on 16 November. That does not establish whether it moved or whether the Foundation has private access. The September 2024 Treasury audit reviews a stated source revision; this review has not reproduced an exact-source build matching the current Treasury deployment. Publishing an audit alone does not resolve current upgrade custody or source-access questions.

  • Advertised source repository
  • September 2024 Treasury audit
  • Source-access check and acquisition history

Can Terra governance resolve these issues?

Yes. Native Terra governance can override the contract-administrator layer without the current administrator’s signature. Two public nodes report Terra v2.22.0, commit e68dd029…, using wasmd v0.54.10. The pinned Terra application assigns Wasm authority to the governance module and forwards administrator, migration and sudo messages to the reviewed handlers.

This is a separate route from a Phoenix Board proposal. It requires an executable Terra governance proposal that passes and executes successfully; a text-only vote does not change the contracts.

Scroll sideways to read all columns.

MechanismWhat it can fixWhat it leaves unresolved
MsgUpdateAdminReassign a named contract’s migration administrator to an approved DAO, multisig or governance address. The reviewed governance policy does not require consent from the existing ERIS administrator.Internal owners, registry roles, fee recipients, executors and voting operators do not change merely because the chain-level administrator changes.
MsgMigrateContractAdopt reviewed replacement code. Its migration can repair internal ownership or role storage and retain the existing contract address and asset balances.The exact code, storage compatibility and migration payload must be reviewed and tested. Claim records, liabilities, IBC callbacks and operating settings must survive as intended. This review has not prepared or simulated a recovery migration.
MsgSudoContractInvoke privileged operations actually implemented in a deployed contract’s sudo entrypoint.It is not a universal command to rewrite ownership or storage. The current Treasury code 3347 and hub code 2726 have no sudo export. A direct sudo call cannot repair either current deployment. Other contracts need their own binary/schema checks.
Ordinary MsgExecuteContractUse powers the contract already grants the governance-module sender—for example supported governance veto or clawback operations.It does not automatically impersonate the ERIS owner or bypass the contract’s ordinary authorization checks. Treasury clawback was advertised, but its exact current payload and behavior still need source/binary validation.
Alliance funding changesChange or stop the relevant reward funding through the chain’s Alliance governance mechanisms.Stopping future inflows does not transfer administrators, recover already-paid funds or settle outstanding depositor and grant claims.

For the Treasury and TLA, use a two-layer remedy

A concrete recovery proposal could first specify the intended administrators for the Treasury, both registries and every affected dependent contract, then resolve internal owners and privileged roles through cooperative accepted transfers or reviewed migrations. Changing only the registry administrator would leave its current internal owner able to operate until that second layer is addressed. The hub and bridge already have Board migration administrators; their remaining internal permissions need separate treatment.

Do not rely on sudo where the required entrypoint is absent. Inspection of the actual downloaded Treasury and hub bytecode found no sudo export; the byte hashes match the chain’s code metadata. This establishes an entrypoint limit, not a full behavioral audit. Governance can still authorize migration through the separate Wasm module handler.

The reviewed governance policy also permits administrator changes and migration when a contract has no administrator. Clearing an admin blocks the ordinary admin route, but does not remove this native governance recovery route.

Recovery power is not immediate protection

Existing keys can still act while a proposal is pending. Recheck deployed code and permissions before execution, test the complete proposal on a faithful fork, and specify post-execution checks for both administrators and internal roles. A proposal being accepted for voting does not prove its messages will execute successfully.

Governance cannot obtain missing private source or credentials merely by changing a contract field, settle legal/IP title, independently certify completed work, or automatically reverse assets already transferred beyond the affected contracts. A recovery proposal must preserve legitimate user claims and be accompanied by the source, maintenance and accountability work described below.

  • Live release evidence, code hashes and exported entrypoints
  • Terra’s Wasm governance authority
  • Terra forwards migration, admin and sudo messages
  • Governance authorization differs from ordinary admin authorization
  • Governance-policy selection
  • Sudo invokes the deployed entrypoint
  • Proposal signer validation and execution limits

What a complete handover should demonstrate

  1. An asset and authority register: each contract, asset claim, funding source, legal owner where established, migration admin, internal owner, operator, fee recipient and downstream dependency.
  2. An approval trail: the grant or ruling authorizing each retained power, applicable deadline, approved variation and any outstanding revenue-sharing or source-delivery obligation.
  3. Verified transfers: executed transactions and accepted ownership, followed by fresh queries of every layer. A new spending controller alone does not prove the upgrade or registry owner changed.
  4. Operational continuity: reproducible deployed builds, licences, source/documentation access, key recovery, maintenance and tested emergency procedures.
  5. Independent limits: disclosed conflicts, independent approval of upgrades and related-party payments, appropriate delay/monitoring controls, and a published route for urgent action.

These are proposed verification requirements, not claims that governance has already enacted them. The two current discussion proposals can use this register to define what must transfer, what may remain with an operator, and which community assets need protection during transition.
